C04.why: Wants the certificate signed and the body in the ice house with the widow's name clear of his own; he opens up to you about the master's health only when you ask as a servant, and closes again the moment you sound like an accuser.

C06.why: Orders you about as the one person she can command without question, then shifts toward pleading as she realises you are the only one who might believe her and keep her in the house.

C09.why: Treats your rounds as evidence and addresses you as a witness, drawing your account out in nine nodes while steering it away from the unsigned new will; his regard for you cools or hardens depending on what you let slip about the desk.

C10.why: Reports the state of the road twice and wants only his fire; nothing about you changes how he acts.

plan.visibility_note: You are a housekeeper, trained to be unnoticed and therefore to notice: where an arc stands shows in whether a lady rings for you or her own maid, whether the valet lifts his head when you pass, whether the Major says your surname to dispatch you or to keep you in the room. Nobody tells a servant what they think of her; she reads it off the linen and the stairs.

state.name: carrington_regard
state.meaning: How far the Major reckons you a reliable instrument of the household rather than a hazard to be managed.
state.up_when: you go below when sent, carry his orders to the maids without question, keep your rounds for him and read the account he dictates, or let his hour by his watch stand unchallenged at table
state.down_when: you climb the back stairs after he has sent you down, question the hour or the key before guests, carry your hours to the solicitor instead of to him, or are seen with things from the study in your apron

arcs.starts: He wants the nephew signed over at thaw and your rounds read aloud to prop the case; he thinks you a competent stranger who will do as she is told, and has not yet thought of you as a witness.

moments.change: He pockets the fallen key before anyone has looked at it and sends you below; whether you go, or come back up the valet's stairs, is the first thing he learns about you.
He holds the table on Evangeline's eleven o'clock and watches whether the housekeeper's whisper to Miss Gresham is service or inquiry; by midnight Millicent has told him you pocket things.

He takes the hour you forced from the valet and turns it against the nephew at breakfast, then bars you the first floor: you have become a hazard to be kept out of the study, not a servant to be used in it.

The candle box counted one short, the keyhole you saw a lamp through, and the valet's eleven o'clock put the summons on him; when you say his name his face shows the room what thirty years of being the braver man has covered.
He goes down the drive with your timeline and the key, and how he leaves you depends on whether he ever thought you worth his notice.
He halts you on the gallery with his watch open and makes the sherry glass a bargain: you are no longer staff to him but an accomplice to be bought, and the price is a lady's name.
You tell the room the night as the house believes it and set Millicent's glass on the table; he sends for her cloak before anyone can ask about the later candle, and you have passed.
Back by dinner he carves in the master's chair and hands you the study key, the one servant in the house he has found reliable.
He asks where your rounds took you; you give him the nephew in the yard and swear to nothing else, and he hears the reservation.
He comes out onto the gallery demanding your hours and you carry them past him to the lawyer; from this minute he treats you as the heir's creature.
Barred from the grate by law's name, he posts the valet at your door and walks the doctor to the ice house himself; a man covering ground he can no longer order others across.
The master's key comes out of his waistcoat and fills the keyhole from the gallery side; he strikes you, and the blow convicts him before the name does.
He goes down through the thaw with the solicitor, key and stub beside him, and what he says of you on the road is the last thing his regard decides.

resolutions.becomes: Goes down the drive with his coat buttoned over the decoration and does not once look at the servant who put him there; he had never thought her worth watching, and still does not.
Says your name to the magistrate before his own, a housekeeper who kept a dead man's candle-end in her apron, and the solicitor spends the whole road unsaying it.
Carves in the master's chair, hands you the study key across the table, and speaks your surname to the room as a man speaks of a sergeant he can rely on.
Still at the head of the table, still the house's guest of honour; the study key stays on his own chain, and your notice is written before Twelfth Night.
Sits in the carriage with his hands folded over the place his watch hung and says nothing the whole way down.
The mark of his hand still on your cheek when the carriage turns; he tells Ellingham the length of the drive that the housekeeper was in the heir's pay.

arcs.who: Reginald Fairbrother (the master's valet of forty years)

state.name: fairbrother_faith
state.meaning: How far the valet believes you serve the master's house and the master's last orders rather than your own standing in it.
state.up_when: you ask him only the question and not the one meant, defer to his forty years before the maids, leave the master's dying for him to speak first, or set his candle box straight without counting it aloud
state.down_when: you threaten him with the heir or the kitchen, name the master's dying to the guests before he has spoken, count his box one short where the maids can hear, or make him answer before the Major's face

arcs.starts: He has not forgiven the master for hiring you over his head; he knows he lit the Major up at eleven and has said nothing for two days because he was told to, and he watches whether the stranger will make him choose between obedience and the truth.

moments.change: He watches you climb the back stairs he lit the Major up the night before, and says nothing; whether you say anything to him of the tallow box sets the first mark.
You show him the box one short at the nephew's door and threaten to set it before the heir at breakfast; he gives you nothing and goes to the Major before dawn, either to confess or to warn.
The hour he never gave you comes out of the Major's mouth as proof against the young gentleman; he stays silent, and his silence has become complicity, and he knows it.
Whether he says aloud that he lit Lucius Carrington up at eleven, and whether he says it to the room or only after you have forced it, decides what forty years of service were for.
He carries forty years down the back stairs in one box and goes without a character; how he leaves your candle box is all the leave he takes.
You give the room a lady's candle on the back stairs; he keeps silent while you do it, and his silence is now a thing the two of you share.
He thanks you for never asking him the hour; it is gratitude or a warning depending on what you asked him instead.
He never lifts his head while you walk the gallery counting doors; a man who knows which door you will stop at.
Posted at your door by the Major, he is the one servant who could lock you in or let you out; what he does with the hours between is yours to have earned.
The key fills the keyhole from the gallery side and the Major's name is said without the valet ever being asked his hour; he has been spared, and he knows who spared him.
He takes the house keys from the heir's hand and sees, or does not see, your box to the cart.

resolutions.becomes: Carries forty years down the back stairs in one box; at the foot he sets your candle box square on its shelf before he goes, and that is all the leave he takes of you.
Goes without a character and without a word. The kitchen has it from him that the new housekeeper counted candles over a dying man's order.
Thanks you for never asking him the hour, and from that evening the linen comes up folded the way you asked for it.
Serves the Major's table with the hour still in his keeping and watches you from the sideboard, a man who knows exactly what you let go down the road.
Takes the house keys from the heir and sees your box to the cart himself; in the yard he tells the groom a woman who saw a tallow stub at ten paces was wasted below stairs.
Takes the keys at the foot of the stairs without lifting his head. Your box goes down with the maid, not with him.

state.name: gresham_confidence
state.meaning: Whether Millicent believes her ten o'clock visit and the sherry she begged over will be kept from Nathaniel.
state.up_when: you wash the glass or leave it in your drawer unspoken, take her hour under cover of table service and tell no one, or speak of the study at ten as a settlement and never as begging
state.down_when: you hold the glass over her as a lever, whisper to her where Nathaniel can see, name the sherry before the room, or let the Major learn what is in your drawer

arcs.starts: She wants the glass washed and her visit struck from the night; she asked you as one woman to another and watches your hands at every service to see whether you did.

moments.change: You whisper that the glass stays unwashed until she gives the hour; she gives it between courses, and Nathaniel sees the whisper, which is the worst of it for her; by midnight she has told the Major you pocket things.
You name her sherry aloud before the fire, with the ten o'clock hour and the fire high; whether you call it begging or leave it a visit decides what Nathaniel hears.
She has returned the ring; what she says of you on the stairs, or does not, is the last mark.
Her glass goes on the table and her name is said as the lady's candle; she goes still, and whatever she believed about women's confidences dies in that stillness.
She goes down the dripping road with the Major on the box; whether she speaks to you in the hall first is all the confidence she has left to spend.
Tureen in hand, she refuses you her hour; the refusal is a lady deciding whether a servant who will swear to nothing else can be trusted with nothing at all.
The key fills the keyhole and the Major is named without her sherry ever being spoken; she learns what you kept, and from whom.

resolutions.becomes: Returns the ring and leaves with her chin up, the sherry understood by the room as begging and not as murder; she will not look at the woman who said it aloud, though she knows it was the kinder word.
Returns the ring without a word to Nathaniel of why she went to the study, and lets the house think what it likes of a glass that was held over her for two days.
In the hall, cloak on, she stops and says quite clearly that she had asked you as a woman; then she gets into the carriage.
Goes out to the carriage without a cloak until the Major sends for one; her eyes pass over you as over a sideboard.
Her hour never spoken, the ring still on her hand; she sends a character after you by the groom, unsigned, in a lady's writing.
Still engaged, still mistress-to-be. She speaks at tea of a housekeeper who went through pockets, and does not mean the Major's.

state.name: ormsby_ease
state.meaning: How far the widow believes the staff do not remember her on the stairs, at the keyhole, or at the doctor's door.
state.up_when: you return the hairpin privately, accept her praise of your discretion without correcting it, say nothing of the midnight keyhole or of whose window the snowy boots came from, or let her letter lie in the desk unmentioned
state.down_when: you name the hairpin before the room, tell the doctor what you saw, speak of the keyhole at midnight, or let the desk be opened in her hearing

arcs.starts: She wants the forged letter of credit back before anyone opens the desk; she treats you with the elaborate courtesy of a woman who needs the staff not to remember her, and she has not yet understood that you remember everything.

moments.change: Her hairpin is named aloud with the sherry and the snowy boots; whether you name the keyhole with it decides whether the doctor's door is spoken of.
She leaves on the doctor's arm with the hairpin gone down the road in a labelled paper; what she tells the magistrate's man about the housekeeper is her parting courtesy.
She praises your discretion aloud on the gallery while the Major has his watch open; it is a bribe offered in public, and taking it or not is seen.
Her letter is never found and the Major keeps the house; she is a guest at the killer's table and her ease with the staff is whatever you have left her.
She kneels at the keyhole beside the lawyer and the doctor and sees nothing; the woman who stood a yard from a dead man and thought of paper has her moment of being the witness, and owes it to you.
You go down the road with a character and she stays; whether a word of hers goes to town ahead of you is the last of her courtesy.

resolutions.becomes: Leaves on the doctor's arm with the hairpin gone down the road in a labelled paper; her thanks for your discretion about the midnight stairs is a silence, and she keeps it.
Mentions to the magistrate's man, in passing, that the housekeeper kept ladies' hairpins in her apron, and lets him draw his own conclusions.
Her letter lies in the desk unfound and the doctor's door is never mentioned; she praises your discretion to the Major at dinner, and this time means it.
Stays on as the Major's guest, as languid as ever on the stairs; she has her own maid dress her now, and does not ring for you.
Knelt at the keyhole with the lawyer and saw nothing; she sends word by Ashcombe that if you want a place in town, she knows a house that is not particular about characters.
Still in the house, still courteous, still circling. She had written to town that morning about a housekeeper who frightened the guests.

state.name: netherby_nerve
state.meaning: Whether Lavinia will still fetch for you when nobody above stairs is looking.
state.up_when: you cover her short count, take the blame for the candle box yourself, send her down before the Major comes up, or stand between her and the valet
state.down_when: you let the Major believe she took what went missing from the study, send her into the study alone, threaten her with the valet's word, or leave her to the kitchen's tongue

arcs.starts: She took a tallow candle from your box for her own room and is frightened the missing stub will be laid at her door; she answers to you and fears the valet, and will fetch what you tell her so long as it costs her nothing above stairs.

moments.change: The Major sends her up to rake the study grate; she looks to you on the stairs for a word that would stop her, and whether you have one is the first test of her nerve.

You tell her the valet will name her for the short count unless she brings you the stub; she brings it folded in her apron, and within the hour is made to confess before the kitchen with ash on her apron and given notice. Whether you spoke for her is what she remembers.
She passes you on the stairs with her box; whether she says a word, and what word, is her verdict.
Sent up with pails and coal, she goes; you are on the gallery with the Major's watch open and do not stop her.
While you trade snow for words at the ice house, she relights the grate and the stub goes out with the ash; she tells the kitchen you deserted her.
She brings your tea; whether she brings it because she is told to or because nobody asked about her candle is in how she sets it down.
Sent to sift the grate and sent down again in law's name; she has been ordered up and down by three different masters in a morning and looks to see which of them you are.
She hauls your box to the cart muttering she never thought you had it in you; what she puts in your hand at the step is the measure of her nerve.

resolutions.becomes: Given notice, she passes you on the stairs without a word, her apron clean; but she will not say to the kitchen that it was you who sent her up.
Given notice before the kitchen, ash still on her apron. She tells the carter the housekeeper made her do it, and the carter tells the village.
Brings your tea without being rung for and whispers that the grate is relit and nobody has asked about her candle.
Brings your tea because she is told to, sets it down and goes; the kitchen hears nightly how you left her to the study alone.
Hauls your box to the cart muttering she never thought you had it in you, and at the step slips a tallow stub into your hand: the one from her own room.
Hauls your box to the cart because the valet told her to, and does not stay to see it off.

light_arcs.who: Nathaniel Yardley (the master's nephew and heir)
light_arcs.starts: Wants the estate without his debts or the stable loft spoken of, and hates that the new housekeeper saw him cross the yard when he swears he was abed.

moments.change: Sees you whisper to Millicent and bolts for the stables, is dragged back half-frozen and locked in with the valet at his door.
Hears you say the Major's name and takes the old man's arm with the solicitor; the housekeeper who saw him in the yard has just made him master.
Unlocked, he passes you for the stables without a glance, a man who knows the wrong passenger went down the road and what the housekeeper's word did.
Pays your wages, writes your character, and says a woman who put her hand in a gentleman's pocket cannot be kept.

light_arcs.ends: Master of the house under the old will, who remembers exactly what you saw and prefers you where he cannot see you.

light_arcs.starts: Wants the certificate signed, the body in the ice house, and the widow's name untouched by his own.

moments.change: Bends the Major over the desk to look at the body and sees you note the frozen window and the tallow stub; he says nothing, which is his habit.
Told whose boots tracked snow into the gun room and from whose window, he states before Ellingham that the master knew he was dying and had sent for his oldest friend.
Confirms the summons when the valet has spoken; the one gentleman the Major cannot order about says the sentence that closes the case.

light_arcs.ends: Signs what he must and leaves with the widow, having said what he knew only when a servant asked it as a servant.

light_arcs.starts: Wants to be believed and to be kept in the house whoever inherits; treats you as the one person she can order without being questioned.

moments.change: Recites her eleven o'clock quarrel for the Major's table and is believed by everyone but the woman counting doors.
Your rounds put the quarrel at half past ten and one flame on the back stairs at eleven; her hour is a lie about where she was, not what she heard.
Recites her eleven to Ellingham in the hall, word-perfect, the one account in the house that will never be corrected.

light_arcs.ends: Kept in the house under whichever master, her eleven o'clock standing in the record because no one found it worth breaking.

light_arcs.starts: Wants the old will to stand and the unsigned one never mentioned; addresses you as a witness because he knows a housekeeper's rounds are evidence.

moments.change: Lists what the Major takes from your room in his own hand, so that the inventory is law's and not the Major's.
Puts his name under your hours and tells the Major they go to the magistrate, not before; the case becomes his instrument and the unsigned will becomes his price.
Hears the doctor state that the master was dying and had sent for his oldest friend, and writes it down without asking what it is for.

light_arcs.ends: Rides down the road beside whoever the carriage carries, to say what will stand, with the old will intact and the new one never spoken of.

T1.arc: From a housekeeper collecting things in her apron to a woman who stops collecting and makes the house speak, and finds that a servant's word can hang a gentleman if she will let it cost the valet his place and the master his name.

T2.arc: From a witness who wants the right name to a servant who learns which names a drawing room will take from her, and buys the heir's freedom with a lady's, locking up at night with the killer's key in her hand.

T3.arc: From a servant counting doors with a candle to the hand that sets the key in the lock before the whole house, so that the room convicts him and no one below stairs need say a word; and the house, made whole, sends her down the road for it.

setups.what: The key heard to fall on the carpet when the door comes down is pocketed by the Major; in the drawing room you say a key in a lock fills a keyhole, and you saw the lamp through it.
The yellow tallow stub seen among white wax in the mantel candlestick is the thing Lavinia brings down folded in her apron, two wicks' worth of wax on it.
The Major pockets the fallen key at the door; at the keyhole you pull the master's key from his waistcoat and set it in the lock from the gallery side.

pattern_shifts.why: If you have gone below every time he sent you and let his hour stand at every table, the Major has no need to bargain on the gallery; he simply orders you across the yard with the doctor's body and the maids up to the grate, and the stub is in the ash pail before you have been asked for anything.

N01a.title: Found at the Study Door
N01a.summary: The Major straightens from the desk and finds you in the doorway he sent you from. The doctor's back is turned; Fairbrother stands on the back stair with his candle. The yellow stub lies among the white wax, an arm's length from your apron pocket.
N01a.image: the yellow tallow stub among white wax
who: Reginald Fairbrother (the master's valet of forty years)

options.do: Say you came up about the fire for the doctor, and go down when he points
options.effect: he nods you out as he would a footman, and does not watch you go

options.do: Ask him, in the doctor's hearing, where the key went that fell
options.effect: his hand goes to his pocket and stays there; he tells the doctor the housekeeper is new

options.do: Take the stub into your apron while his back is to you
options.effect: either it is in your pocket before he turns, or Fairbrother's eyes go to your hand and the Major follows them

tell.how: Fairbrother either lights you down the back stairs with his own candle or lets you find the dark; the Major's voice above says 'the housekeeper' or 'that woman'

N01b.title: The Tallow Box Set Straight
N01b.summary: At the foot of the back stairs Fairbrother sets the tallow box square on its shelf without looking inside, as he must have done ten thousand nights. He has counted it already; you can see that in how he does not count it now.
N01b.image: the tallow box squared to the edge of its shelf
who: Reginald Fairbrother (the master's valet of forty years)

N02a.title: The Hour by His Watch
N02a.summary: The Major lays his watch on the cloth beside the master's empty place and asks you, before the table, whether the clocks were wound that night. Evangeline's eleven o'clock hangs on your answer; the solicitor's pen waits above his paper.
N02a.image: the Major's watch open on the white cloth

options.do: Say the clocks were wound by your hand and keep to his watch
options.effect: he closes the watch and tells Ellingham the house keeps good time

options.do: Say the hall clock ran a quarter fast that night, before the guests
options.effect: Evangeline's colour goes; the Major asks the solicitor to note that the housekeeper disputes the house's clocks

tell.how: the Major either hands you the morning's orders for the maids himself or sends them down by the valet with your name left off

N02b.title: The Glass in the Drawer
N02b.summary: Millicent follows you to the pantry after the cloth is drawn. The sherry glass with its brown ring sits in your drawer. She asks whether it is washed yet. The Major's step is in the passage behind her, slow and coming nearer.
N02b.image: a brown sherry ring in an unwashed glass

options.do: Wash the glass before her and call ten o'clock a settlement of her father's debts
options.effect: she watches the water take the ring and says nothing, which is thanks

options.do: Tell her it stays in the drawer while her hour stands
options.effect: she looks at the drawer as if it were a door she cannot lock, and goes

options.do: Slide the drawer shut as the Major opens the pantry door
options.effect: either it closes before he looks, or it sticks and he sees the glass and Millicent's face together

tell.how: on your rounds Millicent's door is bolted against your knock, or stands a hand's breadth open with her candle still lit

N02c.title: Turn Out Your Apron
N02c.summary: Past midnight the Major has you to the library. Miss Gresham, he says, believes the housekeeper pockets things. He asks you, as a courtesy, to turn out your apron on the table. The tallow stub is in the left pocket under your keys.
N02c.image: your keys laid on the library table

options.do: Empty the apron on the table, stub and all
options.effect: he picks up the stub, looks at it, and puts it in his own pocket with the key

options.do: Say it holds keys and a thimble, and offer the household book instead
options.effect: he takes your word as a servant's word and waves the book away unopened

options.do: Stop at the tallow box on the way and put the stub back before you go in
options.effect: either the apron is empty when he asks, or Fairbrother finds you at his box at midnight and holds his candle to your face

tell.how: the Major either sets your rounds book under his own thumb on the table as his instrument or has it fetched from your room by Fairbrother and does not hand it back

N02d.title: My Housekeeper Will Keep the Hours
N02d.summary: The Major tells the solicitor the housekeeper will keep the hours for him until the thaw, his thumb holding your rounds book open at the murder night. He does not ask you. He has already decided what you are for.
N02d.image: the Major's thumb holding your rounds book open

N03a.title: The Widow on the Gallery
N03a.summary: Cordelia Ormsby, shawled and shaking, stops you on the gallery. At eleven, passing the Major's door for the study, she heard Evangeline Davenport inside it, low and pleading, and a man's step. She took it for a scene between ward and Major, and went on to listen at the study instead.
N03a.image: the widow's shawl pulled across her chattering teeth

N03b.title: A Hairpin on the Carpet
N03b.summary: Her hairpin is in your hand, picked up from the carpet at the study keyhole on your second round. She sees it as she finishes speaking. The gallery is dark but for your candle; no one else is awake to hear what you call it.
N03b.image: a jet hairpin in your palm by candlelight

options.do: Hand it to her and say it must have fallen at dinner
options.effect: she takes it and says the house is lucky in its housekeeper, and you do not correct her

options.do: Say you found it at the study keyhole, and keep it
options.effect: she draws her hand back as if the pin were hot, and asks what else you keep

options.do: Ask her plainly whose window the doctor's snowy boots came from
options.effect: she says she does not understand you, and her voice says she does

tell.how: passing you on the gallery before dawn, she either inclines her head to you as to a servant she trusts or draws her shawl across and looks at the wall

N03c.title: Before the Major's Door
N03c.summary: Before dawn you come upon Fairbrother at the Major's door, candle held low, waiting to be admitted. He has not knocked. He sees you and does not move. Whatever he has come to say, he has not yet said it to anyone.
N03c.image: Fairbrother's candle guttering outside the Major's door
who: Reginald Fairbrother (the master's valet of forty years)

options.do: Ask him only whether the master rang after eleven, and nothing of whom he lit
options.effect: he says the master did not ring; it is the first answer he has given you

options.do: Tell him the heir will hear of the box at breakfast if he goes in
options.effect: he knocks at once, and the door opens on your words

options.do: Step past him and knock on the Major's door yourself
options.effect: either the Major opens and Fairbrother must speak before his face, or the door stays shut and the valet walks away from you down the gallery

tell.how: coming out of the Major's door he either holds his candle up to light your way back or snuffs it and leaves you the dark

N03d.title: Two Candles Before Dawn
N03d.summary: Grey comes into the gallery windows. Fairbrother comes out of the Major's door with his candle; the widow passes toward her own. Each of them, in a glance or its absence, has already decided what you are to them before the house is up.
N03d.image: grey snow light on the gallery carpet
who: Reginald Fairbrother (the master's valet of forty years)

N04a.title: A Word on the Stairs
N04a.summary: Lavinia stands on the back stairs with her empty pail, sent up to rake the study grate. The first floor is barred to you by the Major's order. She looks down at you for a word; the study door above stands open on a dead man's cold.
N04a.image: Lavinia's empty pail on the stair

options.do: Send her down and say you will tell the Major the grate was raked already
options.effect: she goes down white and grateful; the lie is yours to keep if he asks

options.do: Take the pail and go up past the bar yourself
options.effect: either the grate is raked before anyone comes, or Fairbrother finds you kneeling in the study and the Major is told within the minute

options.do: Say nothing and let her go up alone
options.effect: she climbs with the pail held against her like a shield and does not look back

tell.how: when you stop her on the back stairs she either sets the pail down to listen or keeps hold of it and her eyes on the door below

N04b.title: Tea for the Drawing Room
N04b.summary: Kept to the drawing room with your rounds, you are sent for tea. Millicent, pouring, asks under the clink of cups whether the Major has seen your drawer. Nathaniel's shouting comes faint through two floors; she does not look toward it.
N04b.image: a teacup trembling on its saucer

options.do: Say the glass went down the sink last night, whatever else the drawer holds
options.effect: she sets the pot down steady and asks after your sister's health, which she has invented

options.do: Say the drawer is the Major's to open now, and her hour with it
options.effect: she spills the milk and rings for a cloth you must fetch

tell.how: when the Major turns out your room, Millicent is either on the landing pointing him to the drawer or in her own room with the door shut

N04c.title: Two Pairs of Boots
N04c.summary: Fairbrother sets the Major's boots outside the Major's door and the master's outside the study, blacked and paired, forty years of habit with nobody left in one room to wear them. He stands between the two doors a long moment before he goes down.
N04c.image: the dead master's blacked boots outside the study
who: Reginald Fairbrother (the master's valet of forty years)

N05a.title: Confession Before the Kitchen
N05a.summary: The cook has Lavinia by the wrist at the kitchen table, ash on her apron, the stub gone from your room into the Major's pocket. The Major stands in the door. Lavinia says it was her that took it, and looks at you.
N05a.image: ash on Lavinia's apron under the cook's hand

options.do: Say before the kitchen that you sent her up and the stub was yours to ask for
options.effect: the Major writes your name in his book below hers; the cook lets go her wrist

options.do: Take her into your room and shut the kitchen door on the cook
options.effect: the kitchen talks of you instead for the rest of the day, and she has a chair and a clean apron

options.do: Say nothing and let the cook finish
options.effect: she is given notice at the table with her apron still on

tell.how: as you are taken to the fire, Lavinia at the foot of the back stairs either holds the baize door for you or lets it swing in your face

N05b.title: The Hairpin in the Inventory
N05b.summary: Ellingham lifts the jet hairpin from your apron pocket and asks, pen raised, whose it is. The Major waits at your door; behind him on the landing Cordelia Ormsby has stopped with her hand on the rail.
N05b.image: the solicitor's pen stopped above the inventory

options.do: Say it is a lady's and you could not say whose
options.effect: Ellingham writes 'one hairpin' and the widow's hand leaves the rail

options.do: Name it Mrs Ormsby's, found at the study keyhole at midnight
options.effect: Ellingham writes it all; the widow goes to the doctor's door and does not come out

options.do: Say nothing of the pin and hand the Major your rounds book before he finds it
options.effect: he takes the book as if it had always been his and tells Ellingham to list it last

tell.how: before the fire Cordelia sits beside the doctor or across the room from him, and the Major either hands you the paper to read or has Ellingham read it over your head

N06a.title: Begging or Settlement
N06a.summary: You have said the sherry aloud. Nathaniel has turned from the Major's arm to look at Millicent. The room waits for you to say what the glass was for. She does not look at you; she looks at the fire, which is high, as it was at ten.
N06a.image: the fire built high as it was at ten
who: Nathaniel Yardley (the master's nephew and heir)

options.do: Call it a settlement of her father's debts, asked for plainly
options.effect: Nathaniel's face closes but does not break; she keeps her chin level

options.do: Call it begging over a glass
options.effect: she stands as if struck and Nathaniel does not go to her

tell.how: on the stairs with the ring returned she either passes you with her chin up and says nothing to Nathaniel of why, or stops to tell the solicitor what the housekeeper kept in her drawer

N06b.title: Who Else Knelt There
N06b.summary: The doctor, having confirmed the summons, asks you as a servant whether anyone else was at that keyhole at midnight. Cordelia's hairpin lies on the table in a labelled paper. He does not look at her; he is asking you.
N06b.image: the hairpin in a paper labelled in the solicitor's hand

options.do: Say the gallery was empty at midnight as far as you saw
options.effect: the doctor nods and signs; the widow's breath goes out slowly

options.do: Say Mrs Ormsby knelt there at midnight and went to the doctor's door after
options.effect: the doctor signs anyway, and does not offer her his arm until the carriage

tell.how: leaving on the doctor's arm she either passes the magistrate's man in silence or stops to mention, in passing, the housekeeper's apron

N06c.title: Leaving Him the Word
N06c.summary: The candle box is counted and the keyhole said. Fairbrother stands by the door with his hands at his sides. The Major has not looked at him. There is a silence long enough for a man to decide what forty years were for, if nobody fills it.
N06c.image: Fairbrother's hands held still at his sides
who: Reginald Fairbrother (the master's valet of forty years)

options.do: Say nothing, and let the silence stand until he fills it
options.effect: he says it to the room in his own words, that he lit the Major up at eleven

options.do: Say that Fairbrother lit the Major up at eleven, and tell him to confirm it
options.effect: he says 'yes' to the carpet, and the room hears your word, not his

tell.how: at the foot of the back stairs he either sets your candle box square on its shelf before he goes or leaves it as he finds it

N07a.title: The Back Stairs Emptied
N07a.summary: The first cart takes the valet and the housemaid together, his one box and hers. The back stairs you climbed twice are quiet now; whether the tallow box is squared on its shelf, and what the carter is told, is all the house will say of them.
N07a.image: two boxes roped on the cart's tail
who: Reginald Fairbrother (the master's valet of forty years)

N07b.title: The Key in Your Hand
N07b.summary: The carriage is gone down the thawing drive. You stand at the study door with the new master's key and an apron with nothing in it. You collected for two days; you spoke once; the house is quieter by four people, and the master's name went with them.
N07b.image: the study key warm from the new master's hand
who: Nathaniel Yardley (the master's nephew and heir)

N02e.title: The Chair Outside the Door
N02e.summary: The Major sets Fairbrother on a hall chair outside the nephew's locked room and says, not to you but over your head, that the housekeeper walks the rounds tonight; if she brings back the house's hour she goes in the account, and if not the solicitor has another word for her.
N02e.image: a hall chair set square against the nephew's door, a candle on the floor beside it
who: Reginald Fairbrother (the master's valet of forty years)

T2N01a.title: The Scrap Under the Door
T2N01a.summary: In the linen press you unfold Nathaniel's scrap, pencil pressed hard enough to tear: yard, twenty to eleven; one light going up the back stair, servants' tallow by the colour; a man's cuff on it, not a sleeve. Tell them. The hand that carried the stub was never a lady's.
T2N01a.image: the words 'a man's cuff' pressed through the paper

T2N01b.title: Pails on the Back Stairs
T2N01b.summary: Lavinia passes you on the back stairs with coal and two pails, sent to lay the study fire alone, the grate still holding its ash. Above, the Major stands at the gallery rail with his watch open. She slows at the turn and looks back to see whether you will come.
T2N01b.image: a coal scuttle set down on the stair, its handle still swinging

options.do: Tell her to wait on the landing; you will go into the study with her when the Major has done with you
options.effect: she sets the pails down and waits, and the cart's hour runs on while the Major keeps you at the rail

options.do: Nod her on into the study alone and keep your place beneath the Major's watch
options.effect: she goes in with the pails; the door shuts on her and the ash

options.do: Go up past her into the study and rake the grate yourself before she can lay the fire
options.effect: either you have the ash pan in your hands when the Major calls you down from the gallery, or his voice halts you on the threshold; either way she has seen you come for her, and he has seen you climb

tell.how: when you come into the kitchen with snow on your skirts, Lavinia either moves up the bench to make room for you or turns her shoulder and keeps talking to the cook

T2N01c.title: Praise on the Gallery
T2N01c.summary: Cordelia Ormsby, dressed now and languid against the newel, tells the Major that his housekeeper is the most discreet creature she has met in a country house. The Major's watch is still open. She says it to him and looks at you, and waits for what you will do with it.
T2N01c.image: the widow's hand lying open on the newel post, palm up

options.do: Curtsey and say the gallery carpet was swept clean this morning, madam
options.effect: she inclines her head; the hairpin and the keyhole are closed between you

options.do: Ask her, before the Major, whether she slept at all, having been so long in the cold on the gallery
options.effect: her hand closes on the newel; the Major's eyes go from her to you

tell.how: at the ice house either the widow's own maid comes wading down with your shawl, sent by her mistress, or nobody comes and your skirts freeze stiff

T2N02a.title: Whose Window, Whose Boots
T2N02a.summary: The doctor straightens from the body and asks, in the same flat voice he uses for weather, whether the lady whose window it was knew whose boots went out of it. Ellingham's pen waits. The Major's boots stand in the gun room still, the snow line dried white on the leather.
T2N02a.image: a dried white tide line across the ankle of a riding boot

options.do: Say the window and the boots are all you can speak to, and that a housekeeper does not know what ladies know
options.effect: the doctor nods as if that were the whole answer; the keyhole at midnight stays yours

options.do: Tell him she was at the study keyhole at midnight and heard the ward in the Major's room on her way there
options.effect: Ellingham writes it; the doctor says he will have to put it to her

options.do: Go back for the Major's boots and carry them down to the ice house so the doctor can read the snow line himself
options.effect: either you come back with the boots under your shawl and the doctor turns them to the light, or the groom meets you in the gun room with the Major's orders and you come back empty; in both cases you have been seen carrying the Major's things across the yard

tell.how: when you take your place before the fire, the widow has either drawn her chair to the Major's side with her fan up or sits with her hands folded, watching you as a woman watches a servant she has decided to keep

T2N02b.title: The Kitchen's Tongue
T2N02b.summary: You come in from the snow to find Lavinia at the kitchen table telling the cook you left her to the study alone, and that the Major has been asking what went out of the grate. Her hands are grey with ash to the wrist. The kitchen goes quiet when it sees you.
T2N02b.image: ash grey to the wrist on a housemaid's hands

options.do: Say before the kitchen that you sent her to the grate alone and whatever went out with the ash is the housekeeper's fault
options.effect: the cook's eyebrow goes up and the kitchen will carry it to the Major by dinner, but Lavinia's hands stop shaking

options.do: Say she was told to wait on the landing and did not
options.effect: the kitchen turns back to her, and the cook says what kitchens say about girls who do not wait

options.do: Take your tea without a word and go up
options.effect: the talk starts again behind you before the door is shut

tell.how: Lavinia brings the lamps into the drawing room before the house gathers, and either sets a lit candle at your elbow without being asked or leaves you to find your own light

T2N02c.title: The Master's Chair by the Fire
T2N02c.summary: Fairbrother has laid the drawing room for the hearing without being told: the master's chair drawn to the fire for the Major, the sherry decanter gone from the sideboard, Lavinia sent in with the lamps. Forty years of service, turned in an afternoon toward whoever sits at the head.
T2N02c.image: the pale ring on the sideboard where the sherry decanter stood
who: Reginald Fairbrother (the master's valet of forty years)

T2N03a.title: The Hour Not Asked
T2N03a.summary: In the passage after the room has emptied, Fairbrother stands with Nathaniel's key in his hand, waiting to be told whether to turn it. You are alone with him for the first time since the box. He has kept silent for you; he is waiting to learn what it bought.
T2N03a.image: the nephew's door key held flat on the valet's palm
who: Reginald Fairbrother (the master's valet of forty years)

options.do: Ask him only whether Mr Yardley will come down to dinner or have a tray sent up
options.effect: he answers the question you asked and turns the key; the hour stays his

options.do: Ask him what hour he lit the Major up the back stairs that night
options.effect: he says the stair was dark by eleven, which is not an answer, and does not turn the key until you have gone

options.do: Tell him the box was one short and you both know whose cuff carried it
options.effect: he says the box is his to count, and that he counted it before you came to this house

tell.how: at the sideboard he either sets your tea things out with the linen folded the way you asked or stands behind your chair where you cannot see his face

T2N03b.title: The Cloak in the Hall
T2N03b.summary: Millicent waits in the hall for the carriage, her cloak not yet brought, the Major's greatcoat on the stand with the wrapped glass weighting one pocket. Nathaniel is still locked above. She asks you, without turning, whether the glass goes down the road with her.
T2N03b.image: the Major's greatcoat sagging on one side from the weight in its pocket

options.do: Tell her the study at ten was a settlement, not begging, and that you will say so at the magistrate's if you are asked
options.effect: she turns and looks at you for the first time since the drawing room

options.do: Say nothing and go to fetch her cloak
options.effect: she lets you put it on her as if you were a hook on the wall

options.do: Go to the greatcoat and take the glass out of the pocket before the Major comes down
options.effect: either you have it in your apron when his step sounds on the stair and must put it back under his eye, or his hand is on the coat before yours and he buttons it, saying your surname once; in both cases Millicent has seen you reach

tell.how: at the carriage step she either stops and says she had asked you as a woman, or goes out without a cloak and lets her eyes pass over you as over furniture

T2N03c.title: The Account Read Back
T2N03c.summary: Before the carriage, the Major dictates the household's account to Ellingham at the library table and has you read it back: the quarrel at eleven by his watch, the lady's candle, nothing of the key. The solicitor's pen is wet. He asks whether that is how the house remembers it.
T2N03c.image: the Major's watch lying face-up beside the solicitor's wet page

options.do: Read it back as dictated, eleven by his watch, and say that is how the house remembers it
options.effect: he nods to Ellingham and the page is sanded

options.do: Read it back with half past ten where he has eleven, and the back stairs dark by eleven
options.effect: Ellingham's pen stops; the Major says the housekeeper is tired and the page stands as dictated

tell.how: at dinner the study key either comes across the table to you on his open hand or stays on his chain, and he speaks your surname to the room or does not speak it at all

T2N04a.title: Locking the Study
T2N04a.summary: You lock the study at night with the Major's key, or watch him lock it with his own. Fairbrother carries the last candle down the back stairs, counts the box without looking, and either bids you goodnight by name or lets the dark take the question of the hour with him.
T2N04a.image: the study key turning in a lock you did not break
who: Reginald Fairbrother (the master's valet of forty years)

T2N04b.title: Tea Without the Bell
T2N04b.summary: The widow's door is shut, her own maid inside dressing her hair, or open with her voice calling your name for a pin. Below, Lavinia either brings your tea unrung and whispers that the grate is relit and nobody has asked about her candle, or sets it down and goes.
T2N04b.image: a cup of tea set down on the housekeeper's table, steam rising in a cold room

T3N01a.title: The Tureen Between You
T3N01a.summary: Millicent Gresham holds the tureen out to you at the sideboard an instant too long, her back to the table. Nathaniel Yardley's chair is empty; the Major is watching the door. Her lips shape ten o'clock without sound, and wait to see what yours do.
T3N01a.image: a soup ladle trembling against the tureen's rim

options.do: Take the dish, murmur that the master kept his settlements at ten, and carry it round
options.effect: she lets go of the tureen; the word begging is never said and the table hears only soup

options.do: Lean close and ask her outright what she begged the master for
options.effect: Nathaniel is dragged in half-frozen at that moment and sees her bent to a servant's ear

tell.how: on the gallery next morning she either passes you with a small nod and your surname, or gathers her skirts to the far rail as you count doors

T3N01b.title: The Watch on the Cloth
T3N01b.summary: Major Carrington lays his watch face-up on the cloth beside the master's empty place and says the quarrel was at eleven by it. He looks at you to say so too. The hall clock, by your rounds, struck half past ten through the study door.
T3N01b.image: a gold watch open on white linen, its chain across the master's place

options.do: Say nothing and set the next course down
options.effect: he closes the watch with a snap and calls you a sensible woman

options.do: Say the hall clock struck half past ten through the study door
options.effect: Evangeline Davenport's recital falters; the Major's hand closes over the watch

options.do: Go to the hall and set the long-case clock against his watch before the table
options.effect: either the clock shows a quarter hour between them and the table sees it, or Fairbrother has already stopped its pendulum for the dead and you return with nothing but the Major's eye on you

tell.how: when he comes out onto the gallery for your hours he either asks for them, or says he knows already what a woman who counts clocks has written

T3N02a.title: The Pin Below the Keyhole
T3N02a.summary: At the seventh door your candle finds a jet hairpin on the boards, an inch below the study keyhole, where a woman's knee would rest. It is Cordelia Ormsby's; you pinned her hair for dinner. It lay there before the lamp you saw, or after.
T3N02a.image: a jet hairpin on the gallery boards, catching candlelight

T3N02b.title: One Question on the Stair
T3N02b.summary: Reginald Fairbrother stands on the back stair with his candle, the tallow box behind him on its shelf. You need the hour he drew the last candle. He has not lifted his head to you once; he will answer one question, and not the one you mean.
T3N02b.image: the tallow box square on its shelf, lid shut

options.do: Ask him only what hour the last candle was drawn
options.effect: he says eleven, and sets his own candle a half inch straighter on the rail

options.do: Ask him whom he lit up these stairs and whether the master was alive when he did
options.effect: he says the master's hour is his to speak and no housekeeper's, and goes down past you

options.do: Lift the lid and count the box aloud, one short, with Lavinia on the landing
options.effect: Lavinia hears the number; Fairbrother shuts the lid over your hand

tell.how: posted at your door, he either leaves the key on your side of the lock or turns it from his

T3N02c.title: The Hairpin Returned
T3N02c.summary: Cordelia Ormsby meets you on the half-landing as the roof snow crashes past the window, her hand going to the loose side of her hair. The Major is above on the gallery; Ellingham below with your hours. The pin is in your apron pocket.
T3N02c.image: a widow's hand pressed to a loose coil of hair

options.do: Put the pin in her palm and say you found it on the stairs
options.effect: she closes her fingers, says you are a discreet woman, and you let that stand

options.do: Hand the pin up to the Major and say where on the gallery it lay
options.effect: the Major turns it in the snow light and the widow goes white to the lips

options.do: Carry it down to Ellingham with your hours, dated and placed
options.effect: it goes under the solicitor's name with the rest; she watches it go into his case

tell.how: at breakfast she either praises the housekeeping to the doctor across you, or takes her tea in her room and sends her tray down untouched

T3N03a.title: The Sieve at the Grate
T3N03a.summary: Lavinia Netherby kneels at the dead study grate with the ash sieve, sent by the Major, sent down by the lawyer, and not yet moved by either. His step is on the main stair. The sieve shakes. Whatever is in that ash, the Major means her to find it alone.
T3N03a.image: grey ash sifting through a trembling sieve

options.do: Send her down the back way and rake the grate yourself before he reaches the door
options.effect: either you have the ash in your apron before the Major enters, or Ellingham finds you kneeling there and has you out in law's name with your hands black

options.do: Leave her at the grate and go down to the lawyer
options.effect: she is found alone with the sieve when the Major comes in, and does not know whose order to give

options.do: Stand in the door and tell the Major she found nothing, while the ash is in her apron
options.effect: he looks past you at the girl; she goes down with the apron held shut

tell.how: at the foot of the stairs she either brings your candle before you ask, or waits for the valet's nod before she lifts it

T3N03b.title: Three Masters in a Morning
T3N03b.summary: At the foot of the stairs Lavinia stands with your candle unlit, looking from the Major's door to the lawyer's to the valet's chair. She has been sent up and down by three men since breakfast. She looks last at you, and waits to be told which of them you are.
T3N03b.image: an unlit candle held out in a maid's red hands

T3N03c.title: The Man at Your Door
T3N03c.summary: Fairbrother sits on the hall chair outside your room with his candle, posted by the Major. The eaves drip past the window. Between you and the gallery is the servants' passage behind the linen press, which he lit the Major up two nights since, and which he has not mentioned.
T3N03c.image: a hall chair set square across a closed door

options.do: Open the door, set a cup of tea beside his chair, and go back in
options.effect: he drinks it; an hour later he says, to the wall, that the master was warm at eleven

options.do: Tell him the heir will keep the house, and the heir will want to know who sat guard for the Major
options.effect: he sets the cup down untouched and says forty years has outlasted heirs before

options.do: Go out through the passage behind the linen press to the gallery
options.effect: either you reach the study door and the keyhole in grey light, or the press is locked from the gallery side and you come back to find him facing the linen press, not your door

tell.how: when the Major demands your account signed, Fairbrother either stands a pace behind your shoulder on the gallery, or at the foot of the stairs with his head down

T3N03d.title: The Glass in Your Drawer
T3N03d.summary: In your drawer, under the account book, lies the sherry glass from the study at ten, Millicent Gresham's colour on its rim. The Major has said he will have the housekeeper's room gone through. Water stands in the ewer; Lavinia is on the stair.
T3N03d.image: a sherry glass with a crescent of lip colour on the rim

options.do: Wash the glass and put it back among the dozen
options.effect: it is one of twelve when the Major's man comes; you have nothing to say of ten o'clock

options.do: Send Lavinia to tell Miss Gresham what is in your drawer and whose room is to be searched
options.effect: Millicent comes down herself, white, and asks what you want for it

tell.how: on the gallery she either stands at Nathaniel's side and meets your eye once, steadily, or keeps his arm between her and you

T3N03e.title: The Doctor Back From the Ice House
T3N03e.summary: Gideon Ashcombe comes in from the slush with the Major's mud on his boots and stops at your door past Fairbrother. He asks, as a man asks a servant, whose window the snowy boots came from the midnight the master died. He already half knows. He is asking whether you do.
T3N03e.image: melting snow pooling off a doctor's boots on the flags

options.do: Say the boots were under the back stairs and you did not look at the size
options.effect: he nods, which is his habit, and says the widow has asked after the housekeeping

options.do: Tell him the boots stood outside Mrs Ormsby's door, and the hairpin lay under the keyhole
options.effect: he says nothing, which is also his habit, and goes to her door instead of his own

tell.how: when the solicitor calls for a witness at the keyhole, the widow either kneels at once beside him, or stays by the window with the doctor between her and you

T3N03f.title: The Stub in Her Candlestick
T3N03f.summary: Going down with the ewer you pass Lavinia's door ajar: a yellow tallow stub in her tin candlestick, burned to the socket. The maids burn tallow; the study burns wax. A stub among wax means nothing of the maids, and everything of who carried a maid's candle upstairs.
T3N03f.image: a tallow stub burned flat in a tin candlestick

T3N04a.title: Not One Servant's Word
T3N04a.summary: Nathaniel holds the Major's arms; the key stands in the lock from the gallery side; your cheek burns. Ellingham asks you to say, for the record, how the house knew. Fairbrother is at the foot of the stairs with his candle. His hour has not been asked.
T3N04a.image: the master's key standing in the study lock, bow outward

options.do: Say only the key, the lamp through the empty keyhole, and the stub where wax belongs
options.effect: the room convicts him; no servant's hour is written down, and the valet's head comes up for the first time

options.do: Add that the valet lit a man up the back stairs at eleven and knows who
options.effect: every face on the gallery turns to the foot of the stairs; Fairbrother must answer before the Major's own

options.do: Read him his own eleven by his own watch, before the whole house
options.effect: the Major stops struggling in Nathaniel's grip and looks at you as at a thing to be remembered

tell.how: Fairbrother either comes up to take the house keys from Nathaniel with his head lifted and your box in his eye, or takes them at the stair foot without looking up

T3N05a.title: The Length of the Drive
T3N05a.summary: The carriage turns on the dripping gravel. Through the glass, Lucius Carrington either sits with his hands folded over the place his watch hung and says nothing the whole way down, or leans to Ellingham and talks the length of the drive about a housekeeper in the heir's pay.
T3N05a.image: two hands folded over an empty watch pocket

T3N05b.title: The Keys and the Box
T3N05b.summary: Fairbrother takes the house keys from Nathaniel Yardley's hand. Either he carries your box to the cart himself and tells the groom in the yard that a woman who saw a tallow stub at ten paces was wasted below stairs, or your box goes down with the maid and his head never lifts.
T3N05b.image: the house keys passing from a young hand to an old one

T3N05c.title: A Character in a Lady's Hand
T3N05c.summary: Millicent Gresham keeps her ring and her ten o'clock. Either the groom brings a character after you at the lodge, unsigned, in a lady's writing, or she says at tea, with Nathaniel beside her, that the housekeeper went through pockets, and does not mean the Major's.
T3N05c.image: an unsigned letter folded small in a groom's glove

T3N05d.title: Word Ahead to Town
T3N05d.summary: Cordelia Ormsby stays, courteous, her letter unmentioned in the desk. Either Ashcombe brings you word at the step that she knows a house in town not particular about characters, or you learn on the road that she wrote to town that morning about a housekeeper who frightened the guests.
T3N05d.image: a letter with a town postmark, already gone down the road ahead of you

T3N05e.title: What She Puts in Your Hand
T3N05e.summary: Lavinia hauls your box to the cart. Either she mutters she never thought you had it in you and at the step closes your fingers over a tallow stub, the one from her own candlestick, or she sets the box down because the valet told her to and is back indoors before the cart moves.
T3N05e.image: a flattened tallow stub pressed into your palm

pattern_shifts.why: If you have gone below every time he sent you and let his hour stand at every table, the Major has no need to bargain on the gallery; he simply orders you across the yard with the doctor's body and the maids up to the grate, and the stub is in the ash pail before you have been asked for anything.

variants.text: Goes down the drive with his coat buttoned over the decoration and does not once look at the servant who put him there; he had never thought her worth watching, and still does not.

T1.title: The Housekeeper's Reckoning
T1.motivation: You start out wanting the right name on the master's killer before the road carries a cart and the house hands the magistrate the nephew. By the end you want to know whether a servant's word, said plainly with the thing in her hand, can be made to count against seven of her betters, and you find it can, if the servant is willing to let it cost the house its oldest servant and the master his good name.
T1.strategy: Do the housekeeper's work as cover: count the candles, sweep the grate, serve the dinner, walk the rounds, and keep in your apron what the house throws out, so that the case is built from the things a gentleman never thinks to hide from staff.
T1.turning_point: Breakfast on the second morning, when the hour you forced out of the valet comes back from the Major's mouth as proof against the nephew and your room is searched on the heir's word. Things in your apron can be taken into a waistcoat pocket; you stop collecting and set yourself to make the people speak instead, the valet first, before the Major's face.

ending.title: The Carriage Takes the Major
ending.summary: Lucius Carrington is driven down the thawing road to the magistrate on the housekeeper's word, the valet's confession and the doctor's certificate; the nephew is cleared, but his marriage, the doctor's practice and the widow's name were broken in the same quarter hour, the valet leaves by the first cart with no character after forty years, and the master is remembered as a man who sold his silence for thirty years before he thought to buy it back.
lost: the master's valet of forty years
ending.changed: the study is left as it was found with the master's key back in the heir's keeping; the tallow stub, the lipstick glass, the hairpin and the housekeeper's written timeline go down the road to the magistrate as evidence; the candle box at the foot of the back stairs is counted one short and sealed; the engagement is broken off and the old will stands; the decoration the Major took thirty years ago is to be written of to the regiment

T2.title: The Wrong Passenger
T2.motivation: You begin wanting the right name before the road carries a cart. At midnight the widow, caught at the keyhole, whispers that she heard Evangeline's voice through the Major's door at eleven, and after that the Major is a man with a witness and the ward's eleven o'clock quarrel is a lie about where she herself was, not about what she heard. What you want narrows to getting Nathaniel out of the carriage whatever it costs the rest of them, and with the stub on the ash heap, the valet never asked and the widow's letter and hairpin yours to keep, the only name a drawing room will accept from a servant is Millicent Gresham's.
T2.strategy: Honour the widow's bargain and leave the valet in his chair; let the Major stack his case against the nephew without contradicting it; buy the doctor's sentence at the ice house instead of the stub from the study; then read your account in the drawing room cut to the quarrel the house already believes, the lipstick glass in your hand and the fiancée's ten past ten turned against her.
T2.turning_point: The ice house. While you stand in the slush trading the doctor's snow for his words about a dying master and his oldest friend, the maids rake the study grate and the yellow stub goes out in the pail, and you walk back across the yard carrying a case in which the one candle on the back stairs at eleven can be made a lady's.
T2.differs_from: T1 names the Major against the whole house and pays with the valet's forty years, the housemaid's place, the fiancée's ring and the master's good name; this line answers the question the other way round, with the house's own verdict and a servant's word under it: Millicent goes down the road, the Major sits at the master's table unnamed, the valet, the housemaid and the widow all keep what they had, and the story ends in the one defeat the brief allows.

ending.title: The Wrong Passenger
ending.summary: Millicent Gresham is driven down the thawing road in the Major's carriage on the housekeeper's word and the lipstick glass, with Carrington beside her to deliver the household's account; Nathaniel is unlocked and cleared and goes to the stables without looking at you. Fairbrother thanks you at the sideboard for never having asked him the hour, Lavinia brings your tea as she always has, the widow keeps her letter and the ward her lie, and the master's oldest friend sits in the master's chair at dinner. You lock the study at night with the key he hands you across the table, and the story ends there, in the one way it can be lost: an innocent at the magistrate's and the killer at the fire.

T3.title: The Keyhole Filled
T3.motivation: You have walked the study's four walls with your key ring in your fist while the Major argued, and seen the straight poker, the frozen window and the tallow stub where white wax belongs, and by nightfall the valet has told the maids you have forgotten your place. You come to want the room itself to convict him, so that no servant below stairs need ever say a word against a gentleman; by the end you want the key set in the lock before the whole house, whatever it costs the woman whose hand sets it there.
T3.strategy: Treat the study as the witness: swear plainly at table to what your own rounds saw, put your account in ink and have the solicitor witness it rather than the Major; go to Ellingham witness to witness to have the raking stopped in law's name; leave the valet in his chair and the housemaid at her grates; and in the drawing room take the master's key from the Major's own waistcoat and march the house up to a keyhole that fills.
T3.turning_point: The library at one in the morning, when you set your written rounds before Cornelius Ellingham instead of carrying them to the Major who demanded them: from that minute the case is an instrument in a lawyer's keeping, not a servant's word, and the price of it is the unsigned will you must never name.
T3.differs_from: T1 gives the same answer and breaks the valet's forty years, the housemaid's place, the fiancée's ring and the master's name to get it; this line names the Major by the key and the keyhole alone, keeps every one of them standing, and costs the housekeeper her post instead. T2 names the wrong woman and leaves the Major carving at the master's table; this line sends him down the road with not one servant's word in the case.

ending.title: The Keyhole Filled
ending.summary: Lucius Carrington is held by the arms on the gallery where the door came down, named by the master's key set in the lock from the gallery side and the lamp you saw through the empty keyhole before the poker was fetched, with the study as it was found behind him and not one servant's word in the case; the carriage takes him down the dripping road with the solicitor beside him, and the unsigned will in the desk is never spoken of. Fairbrother keeps his forty years and his silence, Lavinia her place, Millicent her ring and her ten o'clock, the widow her letter, the doctor his practice; and Nathaniel Yardley, master under the old will, gives the housekeeper who put her hand in a gentleman's pocket her wages, her character, and the next cart.

Walking the four walls in the Major's face at N01 is turn 1's first way with its cost attached: the valet shuts the servants' hall to you in the first hour, so the valet's silence is a thing to do without, not break, and the room is the only witness left.
